questions.question:
Consider the system of linear equations:
$x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta + z = \sin\theta$
$x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta + z = \cos\theta$
$x + y + z = 1$

If the system has infinitely many solutions and $\theta \in [0, 4\pi]$, then the sum of the values of $\dfrac{4\theta}{\pi}$ for all valid $\theta$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix $\Delta$ must be zero.
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 1 \\ \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$\sin\theta(\sin\theta - 1) - \cos\theta(\cos\theta - 1) + 1(\cos\theta - \sin\theta) = 0$
$\Rightarrow \sin^2\theta - \sin\theta - \cos^2\theta + \cos\theta + \cos\theta - \sin\theta = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta) - 2(\sin\theta - \cos\theta) = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\sin\theta - \cos\theta)(\sin\theta + \cos\theta) - 2(\sin\theta - \cos\theta) = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\sin\theta - \cos\theta)(\sin\theta + \cos\theta - 2) = 0$

Since the maximum value of $\sin\theta + \cos\theta$ is $\sqrt{2}$, the factor $(\sin\theta + \cos\theta - 2)$ can never be zero for any real $\theta$.
Therefore, we must have:
$\sin\theta - \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = 1$

For $\tan\theta = 1$, it is easy to verify that $\Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0$, confirming infinitely many solutions.
The solutions for $\tan\theta = 1$ in the domain $[0, 4\pi]$ are:
$\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{9\pi}{4}, \dfrac{13\pi}{4}$

The corresponding values of $\dfrac{4\theta}{\pi}$ are $1, 5, 9, 13$.
Sum $= 1 + 5 + 9 + 13 = 28$.

Answer: 28

(where $\text{Tr}(M)$ denotes the trace of matrix $M$ and $\text{adj}(A)$ denotes the adjoint of matrix $A$)
questions.solution:
For the system $AX = B$ to have infinitely many solutions, we must have $|A| = 0$.

$|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2(4 - \alpha) - 1(2 - 3\alpha) + 1(1 - 6) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 8 - 2\alpha - 2 + 3\alpha - 5 = 0$
$\Rightarrow \alpha + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = -1$

Substitute $\alpha = -1$ into the system of equations:
$2x + y + z = 1$
$x + 2y - z = 2$
$3x + y + 2z = p$

For infinitely many solutions, $D_x = D_y = D_z = 0$. Let us check $D_y = 0$:
$D_y = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & p & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2(4 + p) - 1(2 + 3) + 1(p - 6) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 8 + 2p - 5 + p - 6 = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3p - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow p = 1$

Now, we find the trace of $\text{adj}(A)$, which is the sum of the diagonal cofactors $C_{11}, C_{22}, C_{33}$ of matrix $A$:
$C_{11} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 4 - (-1) = 5$
$C_{22} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 4 - 3 = 1$
$C_{33} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 4 - 1 = 3$
$\text{Tr}(\text{adj}(A)) = C_{11} + C_{22} + C_{33} = 5 + 1 + 3 = 9$

Finally, the required value is:
$\alpha^2 + p^2 + \text{Tr}(\text{adj}(A)) = (-1)^2 + (1)^2 + 9 = 1 + 1 + 9 = 11$

Answer: $11$

This requires the determinant of the coefficient matrix to be zero:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & \alpha \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$2(\alpha + 2) - 1(\alpha - 1) - 1(-2 - 1) = 0$
$2\alpha + 4 - \alpha + 1 + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = -8$

$a + b = -2$

$3(3) - 5(4) = 9 - 20 = -11$

For the planes to form a prism (no common line of intersection), the constant term of the third plane must not match this value.
Therefore, $\beta \neq -11$.

Answer: $\alpha = -8, \beta \neq -11$

$2x + 5y - 4z = 5$
$4x + 9y + \lambda z = \mu$
has no solution, then which of the following can be the ordered pair $(\lambda, \mu)$?
questions.solution:
For the system to have no solution, we must have $\Delta = 0$ and at least one of $\Delta_1, \Delta_2, \Delta_3 eq 0$.

$\Delta = egin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \ 2 & 5 & -4 \ 4 & 9 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 1(5\lambda + 36) - 2(2\lambda + 16) - 3(18 - 20) = \lambda + 10$.

Setting $\Delta = 0$ gives $\lambda = -10$.

Now, evaluate $\Delta_3$:
$\Delta_3 = egin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \ 2 & 5 & 5 \ 4 & 9 & \mu \end{vmatrix} = 1(5\mu - 45) - 2(2\mu - 20) + 4(18 - 20) = \mu - 13$.

For the system to be inconsistent (no solution), we require $\Delta_3 eq 0$, which implies $\mu - 13 eq 0 \Rightarrow \mu eq 13$.

Hence, the conditions are $\lambda = -10$ and $\mu eq 13$. Among the given options, the pair $(-10, 15)$ satisfies these conditions.

Answer: $(-10, 15)$

Consider the system of linear equations:
$x + y + z = 1$
$4x + 5y + \alpha z = 2$
$16x + 25y + \alpha^2 z = 5$

Let the system be inconsistent for exactly two values of $\alpha$, say $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$. If $A = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_1 & 1 \\ 0 & \alpha_2 \end{bmatrix}$, then the trace of the matrix $A^3$ is
questions.solution:
For the system to be inconsistent, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 5 & \alpha \\ 16 & 25 & \alpha^2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying $C_2 \rightarrow C_2 - C_1$ and $C_3 \rightarrow C_3 - C_1$:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & \alpha - 4 \\ 16 & 9 & \alpha^2 - 16 \end{vmatrix} = (\alpha^2 - 16) - 9(\alpha - 4) = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\alpha - 4)(\alpha + 4 - 9) = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\alpha - 4)(\alpha - 5) = 0$
Thus, $\alpha = 4$ or $\alpha = 5$.

We must verify that these values make the system inconsistent.
For $\alpha = 4$, the equations are $x+y+z=1$, $4x+5y+4z=2$, and $16x+25y+16z=5$.
From the first two equations, $y = -2$ and $x+z = 3$. Substituting into the third equation gives $16(3) + 25(-2) = 48 - 50 = -2 \neq 5$. So the system is inconsistent.
For $\alpha = 5$, the equations are $x+y+z=1$, $4x+5y+5z=2$, and $16x+25y+25z=5$.
From the first two equations, $y+z = -2$ and $x = 3$. Substituting into the third equation gives $16(3) + 25(-2) = -2 \neq 5$. So the system is inconsistent.

Thus, $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are $4$ and $5$.
The matrix is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ (or vice versa).
Since $A$ is an upper triangular matrix, its eigenvalues are its diagonal elements, $4$ and $5$.
The eigenvalues of $A^3$ are $4^3 = 64$ and $5^3 = 125$.
The trace of $A^3$ is the sum of its eigenvalues:
$\text{Trace}(A^3) = 64 + 125 = 189$.

Answer: $189$

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -7 & a \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$1(a - (-7)) - (-2)(2a - 1) + 3(-14 - 1) = 0$

$\Rightarrow 5a - 40 = 0$
$\Rightarrow a = 8$

$\Rightarrow 24 + 7b + 96 - 2b - 135 = 0$
$\Rightarrow 5b - 15 = 0$
$\Rightarrow b = 3$

Therefore, $a + b = 8 + 3 = 11$.



Answer: $11$

questions.question: Let $D(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \sin x & \ln(1+x) & e^x-1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x & x & 2x \end{vmatrix}$ and $L = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{D(x)}{x^3}$. Then the value of $12L$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given $D(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \sin x & \ln(1+x) & e^x-1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x & x & 2x \end{vmatrix}$.

Applying the column operation $C_1 \to C_1 - C_2$, we get:
$D(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \sin x - \ln(1+x) & \ln(1+x) & e^x-1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & x & 2x \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first column:
$D(x) = (\sin x - \ln(1+x)) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ x & 2x \end{vmatrix} - 0 + 0$
$D(x) = (\sin x - \ln(1+x))(2x - x) = x(\sin x - \ln(1+x))$

Now, substitute $D(x)$ into the limit:
$L = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{D(x)}{x^3} = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{x(\sin x - \ln(1+x))}{x^3} = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin x - \ln(1+x)}{x^2}$

This is a $\dfrac{0}{0}$ indeterminate form. Using L'Hôpital's rule:
$L = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\cos x - \dfrac{1}{1+x}}{2x}$

This is again a $\dfrac{0}{0}$ form. Applying L'Hôpital's rule a second time:
$L = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{-\sin x + \dfrac{1}{(1+x)^2}}{2} = \dfrac{-0 + 1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Therefore, the value of $12L = 12 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 6$.

Answer: 6

questions.question:
A fair six-sided die is rolled three times, and the outcomes are recorded as $a$, $b$, and $c$, respectively. Let $p$ be the probability that the system of linear equations
$\begin{array}{l} x + y + z = a \\ x + 2y + 3z = b \\ 2x + 3y + 4z = c \end{array}$
has infinitely many solutions. Then the value of $72p$ is
questions.solution:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 1(8 - 9) - 1(4 - 6) + 1(3 - 4) = -1 + 2 - 1 = 0$

Since $\Delta = 0$, the system will have infinitely many solutions if the equations are linearly dependent. Observing the coefficients, we see that the third equation's left-hand side is exactly the sum of the first two:
$(x + y + z) + (x + 2y + 3z) = 2x + 3y + 4z$

For the system to be consistent (and thus have infinitely many solutions), the constants must satisfy the same relationship:
$c = a + b$

The variables $a$, $b$, and $c$ are outcomes of rolling a fair six-sided die, so $a, b, c \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. We need to find the number of pairs $(a, b)$ such that their sum $c$ is at most $6$.

If $c = 2$, $(a, b)$ can be $(1, 1)\rightarrow 1$ outcome.
If $c = 3$, $(a, b)$ can be $(1, 2), (2, 1)\rightarrow 2$ outcomes.
If $c = 4$, $(a, b)$ can be $(1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1)\rightarrow 3$ outcomes.
If $c = 5$, $(a, b)$ can be $(1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1)\rightarrow 4$ outcomes.
If $c = 6$, $(a, b)$ can be $(1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 2), (5, 1)\rightarrow 5$ outcomes.

Total number of favorable outcomes = $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$.
The total number of possible outcomes when rolling three dice is $6^3 = 216$.

The probability $p$ is therefore:
$p = \dfrac{15}{216} = \dfrac{5}{72}$

Thus, $72p = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{72} = 5$.

Answer: $5$

questions.question:
The number of real roots of the equation

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & x+1 & x^2+x+1 \\ 1 & 2 & x^2+2 \\ 3x & 4x-1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

is
questions.solution:
Given the equation:

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & x+1 & x^2+x+1 \\ 1 & 2 & x^2+2 \\ 3x & 4x-1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying the row operation $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 - R_2$:

$\begin{vmatrix} 0 & x-1 & x-1 \\ 1 & 2 & x^2+2 \\ 3x & 4x-1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying the column operation $C_2 \rightarrow C_2 - C_3$:

$\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & x-1 \\ 1 & -x^2 & x^2+2 \\ 3x & 4x-1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$(x-1) [1(4x - 1) - (-x^2)(3x)] = 0$

$\Rightarrow (x-1) (3x^3 + 4x - 1) = 0$

This gives $x = 1$ as one real root.

For the second factor, let $g(x) = 3x^3 + 4x - 1 = 0$.

Differentiating with respect to $x$, we get $g'(x) = 9x^2 + 4$.

Since $g'(x) > 0$ for all real $x$, the function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing. A strictly increasing cubic polynomial has exactly one real root.

Also, $g(1) = 3(1)^3 + 4(1) - 1 = 6 \neq 0$, so the root of $g(x) = 0$ is distinct from $x = 1$.

Thus, the equation has exactly $2$ real roots.

Answer: $2$

If the vector equation $x\vec{u} + y\vec{v} + z\vec{w} = \vec{b}$ has infinitely many solutions for the scalars $x, y, z$, then the sum of $(\alpha + 2\beta)^2$ over all possible ordered pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ is
questions.question: Let $\vec{u} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \beta\hat{k}$, $\vec{v} = \hat{i} + \beta\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{w} = \beta\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \alpha\hat{j} + \hat{k}$. If the vector equation $x\vec{u} + y\vec{v} + z\vec{w} = \vec{b}$ has infinitely many solutions for the scalars $x, y, z$, then the sum of $(\alpha + 2\beta)^2$ over all possible ordered pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ is
questions.solution:
Equating the components of the vectors, we get the system of linear equations:
$x + y + \beta z = 1$
$x + \beta y + z = \alpha$
$\beta x + y + z = 1$

For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & \beta \\ 1 & \beta & 1 \\ \beta & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant:
$1(\beta - 1) - 1(1 - \beta) + \beta(1 - \beta^2) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2(\beta - 1) - \beta(\beta - 1)(\beta + 1) = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\beta - 1)(2 - \beta^2 - \beta) = 0$
$\Rightarrow -(\beta - 1)^2(\beta + 2) = 0$
Thus, $\beta = 1$ or $\beta = -2$.

Case 1: $\beta = 1$
The equations become identical:
$x + y + z = 1$
$x + y + z = \alpha$
$x + y + z = 1$
For infinitely many solutions, we must have $\alpha = 1$. This gives the pair $(1, 1)$.

Case 2: $\beta = -2$
The equations are:
$x + y - 2z = 1$
$x - 2y + z = \alpha$
$-2x + y + z = 1$
Adding all three equations gives:
$0 = \alpha + 2 \Rightarrow \alpha = -2$
This gives the pair $(-2, -2)$.

The possible pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ are $(1, 1)$ and $(-2, -2)$.
For $(1, 1)$: $(\alpha + 2\beta)^2 = (1 + 2)^2 = 9$
For $(-2, -2)$: $(\alpha + 2\beta)^2 = (-2 - 4)^2 = 36$
The sum of these values is $9 + 36 = 45$.

Answer: $45$

Let the homogeneous system of linear equations
$(\sin \theta)x - y + z = 0$
$(\cos \theta)x + 4y + 3z = 0$
$2x + 7y + 7z = 0$
have non-trivial solutions. The number of values of $\theta$ in the interval $[0, 2\pi]$ is
questions.solution:
For a homogeneous system to have non-trivial solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} \sin \theta & -1 & 1 \\ \cos \theta & 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 7 & 7 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant:
$\sin \theta (28 - 21) - (-1)(7\cos \theta - 6) + 1(7\cos \theta - 8) = 0$
$7\sin \theta + 7\cos \theta - 6 + 7\cos \theta - 8 = 0$
$7\sin \theta + 14\cos \theta - 14 = 0$
$\sin \theta + 2\cos \theta = 2$

Rearranging gives $\sin \theta = 2(1 - \cos \theta)$.
Squaring both sides:
$\sin^2 \theta = 4(1 - 2\cos \theta + \cos^2 \theta)$
$1 - \cos^2 \theta = 4 - 8\cos \theta + 4\cos^2 \theta$
$5\cos^2 \theta - 8\cos \theta + 3 = 0$

Factoring the quadratic equation:
$(5\cos \theta - 3)(\cos \theta - 1) = 0$

Case 1: $\cos \theta = 1$
This gives $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = 2\pi$. Substituting back into $\sin \theta + 2\cos \theta = 2$ yields $\sin \theta = 0$, which is satisfied for both values.

Case 2: $\cos \theta = \dfrac{3}{5}$
Substituting into the original equation $\sin \theta + 2\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = 2$, we get $\sin \theta = \dfrac{4}{5}$.
Since both $\sin \theta$ and $\cos \theta$ are positive, $\theta$ must lie in the first quadrant. This gives exactly one solution in $[0, 2\pi]$. (The fourth quadrant angle where $\cos \theta = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\sin \theta = -\dfrac{4}{5}$ is an extraneous root introduced by squaring).

Thus, the valid solutions are $\theta = 0, 2\pi$, and one angle in the first quadrant. The total number of solutions is $3$.

Answer: $3$

If $D(-12) = 0$, then the value of $c$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let the terms of the Arithmetic Progression be $a = 4-d$, $b = 4$, and $c = 4+d$, since their sum is $12$. As $a < b < c$, the common difference $d > 0$.

Expanding the determinant $D(x)$ by applying $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 - R_2$ and $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_3$:
$D(x) = \begin{vmatrix} a & -b & 0 \\ 0 & b & -c \\ x & x & x+c \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along the first row gives:
$D(x) = abc + x(ab + bc + ca)$

Now, express the coefficients in terms of $d$:
$abc = (4-d)(4)(4+d) = 4(16-d^2) = 64 - 4d^2$

$ab + bc + ca = (4-d)4 + 4(4+d) + (4-d)(4+d)$
$= 16 - 4d + 16 + 4d + 16 - d^2 = 48 - d^2$

Substitute these into $D(x)$:
$D(x) = (64 - 4d^2) + x(48 - d^2)$

We are given $D(-12) = 0$:
$64 - 4d^2 - 12(48 - d^2) = 0$
$64 - 4d^2 - 576 + 12d^2 = 0$
$8d^2 - 512 = 0$
$8d^2 = 512 \Rightarrow d^2 = 64$

Since $d > 0$, we have $d = 8$.

The value of $c$ is $4 + d = 4 + 8 = 12$.

Answer: $12$

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & \alpha & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ \beta \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$. If the system of equations $AX = B$ has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $\alpha + \beta + \text{trace}(\text{adj}(A))$ is equal to
questions.question: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & \alpha & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ \beta \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$. If the system of equations $AX = B$ has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $\alpha + \beta + \text{trace}(\text{adj}(A))$ is equal to
questions.solution:
For the system $AX = B$ to have infinitely many solutions, we must have $\det(A) = 0$.

$\det(A) = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & \alpha & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$1(\alpha^2 - 6) - 2(2\alpha - 3) + 1(4 - \alpha) = 0$
$\Rightarrow \alpha^2 - 6 - 4\alpha + 6 + 4 - \alpha = 0$
$\Rightarrow \alpha^2 - 5\alpha + 4 = 0$
$\Rightarrow (\alpha - 1)(\alpha - 4) = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 1 \text{ or } \alpha = 4$

If $\alpha = 1$, the first and third rows of the augmented matrix correspond to the equations $x + 2y + z = 3$ and $x + 2y + z = 9$, which are inconsistent. Thus, $\alpha = 4$.

For $\alpha = 4$, the system is:
$x + 2y + z = 3$ (i)
$2x + 4y + 3z = \beta$ (ii)
$x + 2y + 4z = 9$ (iii)

Subtracting (i) from (iii) gives $3z = 6 \Rightarrow z = 2$.
Substituting $z = 2$ into (i) gives $x + 2y = 1$.
Now substituting $x + 2y = 1$ and $z = 2$ into (ii):
$2(x + 2y) + 3z = \beta$
$\Rightarrow 2(1) + 3(2) = \beta \Rightarrow \beta = 8$

The trace of $\text{adj}(A)$ is the sum of the diagonal cofactors of $A$. With $\alpha = 4$:
$C_{11} = (4)(4) - (3)(2) = 10$
$C_{22} = (1)(4) - (1)(1) = 3$
$C_{33} = (1)(4) - (2)(2) = 0$

$\text{trace}(\text{adj}(A)) = 10 + 3 + 0 = 13$

Hence, $\alpha + \beta + \text{trace}(\text{adj}(A)) = 4 + 8 + 13 = 25$.

Answer: $25$

For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & \lambda^2 - 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$\Delta = 1(2\lambda^2 - 2 - 9) - 1(\lambda^2 - 1 - 6) + 1(3 - 4)$
$\Delta = (2\lambda^2 - 11) - (\lambda^2 - 7) - 1$
$\Delta = \lambda^2 - 5$

Setting $\Delta = 0$ gives $\lambda^2 = 5$.

$\Delta_z = (2\mu - 13) - (\mu - 9) - 2$
$\Delta_z = \mu - 6$

Setting $\Delta_z = 0$ gives $\mu = 6$.

Therefore, $\lambda^2 + \mu^2 = 5 + 36 = 41$.

Answer: $41$

Let $S$ be the set of all values of $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ for which the system of linear equations

$x + (\sin \theta)y + (\cos \theta)z = 0$
$(\sin \theta)x + y + (\sin \theta)z = 0$
$(\cos \theta)x + (\sin \theta)y + z = 0$

has a non-trivial solution. Then the sum of all elements of $S$ is
questions.solution:
For a homogeneous system of linear equations to have a non-trivial solution, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta & 1 & \sin\theta \\ \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant:
$1(1 - \sin^2\theta) - \sin\theta(\sin\theta - \sin\theta\cos\theta) + \cos\theta(\sin^2\theta - \cos\theta) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 1 - \sin^2\theta - \sin^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\cos\theta + \sin^2\theta\cos\theta - \cos^2\theta = 0$
$\Rightarrow (1 - \cos^2\theta) - 2\sin^2\theta + 2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta = 0$
$\Rightarrow \sin^2\theta - 2\sin^2\theta + 2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta = 0$
$\Rightarrow -\sin^2\theta + 2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta = 0$
$\Rightarrow \sin^2\theta(2\cos\theta - 1) = 0$

This gives $\sin\theta = 0$ or $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Given $\theta \in [0, \pi]$:
If $\sin\theta = 0$, then $\theta = 0, \pi$.
If $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$, then $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

The sum of all possible values of $\theta$ is $0 + \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.



Answer: $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$

The graph of $y = D(x)$ in the $xy$-plane is a straight line passing through the points $(1, 15)$ and $(-1, -5)$. If $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = 6$, then the value of $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3$ is equal to
questions.question:
Let $D(x) = \begin{vmatrix} x+\alpha & x & x \\ x & x+\beta & x \\ x & x & x+\gamma \end{vmatrix}$.

The graph of $y = D(x)$ in the $xy$-plane is a straight line passing through the points $(1, 15)$ and $(-1, -5)$. If $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = 6$, then the value of $\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Expanding the given determinant, we apply the operations $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 - R_2$ and $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_3$:

$D(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \alpha & -\beta & 0 \\ 0 & \beta & -\gamma \\ x & x & x+\gamma \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along the first row:
$D(x) = \alpha[\beta(x+\gamma) - (-\gamma)(x)] - (-\beta)[0 - (-\gamma)(x)]$
$D(x) = \alpha(\beta x + \beta\gamma + \gamma x) + \beta(\gamma x)$
$D(x) = \alpha\beta\gamma + x(\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha)$

This shows $y = D(x)$ is a linear function. We are given that it passes through $(1, 15)$ and $(-1, -5)$.
Substituting $x = 1$:
$\alpha\beta\gamma + (\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha) = 15$ ... (i)

Substituting $x = -1$:
$\alpha\beta\gamma - (\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha) = -5$ ... (ii)

Adding (i) and (ii):
$2\alpha\beta\gamma = 10 \Rightarrow \alpha\beta\gamma = 5$

Subtracting (ii) from (i):
$2(\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha) = 20 \Rightarrow \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = 10$

We are given $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = 6$.
Using the algebraic identity:
$\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 - 3\alpha\beta\gamma = (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)[(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2 - 3(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)]$

Substitute the known values:
$\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 - 3(5) = 6[6^2 - 3(10)]$
$\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 - 15 = 6[36 - 30]$
$\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 - 15 = 36$
$\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 = 51$

Answer: $51$

$x + y + z = 2$
$2x + 3y + az = 3$
$x + ay + 3z = b$
has infinitely many solutions. The sum of $(a^2 + b^2)$ over all $(a, b) \in S$ is
questions.solution:
For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta = \Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0$.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & a \\ 1 & a & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 1(9 - a^2) - 1(6 - a) + 1(2a - 3) = -a^2 + 3a$

Setting $\Delta = 0 \Rightarrow a(3 - a) = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $a = 3$.

Case 1: $a = 0$
The system becomes:
$x + y + z = 2$
$2x + 3y = 3$
$x + 3z = b$
For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta_x = 0$:
$\Delta_x = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 & 0 \\ b & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 2(9) - 1(9) + 1(-3b) = 9 - 3b$
$9 - 3b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 3$.
For $a = 0, b = 3$, it can be easily verified that $\Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0$.
So, $(0, 3) \in S$.

Case 2: $a = 3$
The system becomes:
$x + y + z = 2$
$2x + 3y + 3z = 3$
$x + 3y + 3z = b$
For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta_y = 0$:
$\Delta_y = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & b & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 1(9 - 3b) - 2(6 - 3) + 1(2b - 3) = -b$
$-b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 0$.
For $a = 3, b = 0$, it can be verified that $\Delta_x = \Delta_z = 0$.
So, $(3, 0) \in S$.

The valid pairs are $(0, 3)$ and $(3, 0)$.
Sum of $(a^2 + b^2) = (0^2 + 3^2) + (3^2 + 0^2) = 9 + 9 = 18$.

Answer: $18$

First, set $\Delta = 0$:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 11 & -7 & \alpha \end{vmatrix} = 0$

$\Rightarrow 3\beta - 15 - 9 = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3\beta = 24 \Rightarrow \beta = 8$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha + \beta = 10 + 8 = 18$.

Answer: $18$

x+y-z=4

4x+y-7z=13

questions.solution:
Given the system of equations:
x+y-z=4     ...(1)
2x-y-5z=5   ...(2)

Since the system has infinitely many solutions, the third equation is a linear combination of the first two and provides no new information. We can solve for x and y in terms of z using just the first two equations.

Adding equation (1) and equation (2) to eliminate y:
(x+y-z)+(2x-y-5z)=4+5
3x-6z=9

Dividing by 3:
x-2z=3⇒x=2z+3
Comparing this with x=az+b, we get a=2 and b=3.

Substitute x=2z+3 back into equation (1):
(2z+3)+y-z=4
z+3+y=4
y=-z+1
Comparing this with y=cz+d, we get c=-1 and d=1.

Finally, calculate the required sum:
a2+b2+c2+d2=(2)2+(3)2+(-1)2+(1)2
=4+9+1+1=15.

Answer: 15

$\alpha x + y + z = 1$

$x + \alpha y + z = k$

questions.solution:
First, we solve the given determinant equation:

$\begin{vmatrix} x & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & x & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & x \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying $C_1 \to C_1 + C_2 + C_3$:

$\begin{vmatrix} x+2 & 1 & 1 \\ x+2 & x & 1 \\ x+2 & 1 & x \end{vmatrix} = 0$

$(x+2) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & x & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & x \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying $R_2 \to R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$:

$(x+2) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & x-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & x-1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

$(x+2)(x-1)^2 = 0$

The distinct roots are $1$ and $-2$. Since $\alpha > \beta$, we have $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = -2$.

Substituting these values into the given system of equations, we get:

$x + y + z = 1$

$x + y + z = k$

$x + y + z = -2$

The first and third equations represent parallel, non-coincident planes ($x+y+z=1$ and $x+y+z=-2$). Since these two planes never intersect, the system of equations is unconditionally inconsistent.

Thus, there is no real value of $k$ for which the system can have any solution, let alone infinitely many solutions.

The number of values of $k$ is $0$.

Answer: $0$

$(\sin 2\theta)x + (\sin 2\theta)y + (2+\sin 2\theta)z = 7$

questions.question:
Consider the following system of linear equations:
$(2+\sin^2 \theta)x + (\sin^2 \theta)y + (\sin^2 \theta)z = 1$
$(\cos^2 \theta)x + (2+\cos^2 \theta)y + (\cos^2 \theta)z = 4$
$(\sin 2\theta)x + (\sin 2\theta)y + (2+\sin 2\theta)z = 7$

The maximum value of $x + y + z$ as $\theta$ varies over all real numbers is
questions.solution:
Let the given system of equations be:
$(2+\sin^2 \theta)x + (\sin^2 \theta)y + (\sin^2 \theta)z = 1$ ... (i)
$(\cos^2 \theta)x + (2+\cos^2 \theta)y + (\cos^2 \theta)z = 4$ ... (ii)
$(\sin 2\theta)x + (\sin 2\theta)y + (2+\sin 2\theta)z = 7$ ... (iii)

Adding equations (i), (ii), and (iii) vertically, we sum the coefficients of $x$, $y$, and $z$ respectively:
Coefficient of $x$: $(2+\sin^2 \theta) + \cos^2 \theta + \sin 2\theta = 2 + 1 + \sin 2\theta = 3 + \sin 2\theta$
Coefficient of $y$: \sin^2 \theta + (2+\cos^2 \theta) + \sin 2\theta = 3 + \sin 2\theta
Coefficient of $z$: \sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta + (2+\sin 2\theta) = 3 + \sin 2\theta

Thus, the sum of the three equations yields:
$(3 + \sin 2\theta)x + (3 + \sin 2\theta)y + (3 + \sin 2\theta)z = 1 + 4 + 7$
$\Rightarrow (3 + \sin 2\theta)(x + y + z) = 12$
$\Rightarrow x + y + z = \dfrac{12}{3 + \sin 2\theta}$

To maximize the value of $x + y + z$, the denominator $3 + \sin 2\theta$ must be minimized.
The minimum value of $\sin 2\theta$ is $-1$.
Therefore, the minimum value of the denominator is $3 - 1 = 2$.

Maximum value of $x + y + z = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6$.

Answer: $6$

If the matrix equation
x \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} + z \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ \alpha \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ \beta \end{bmatrix}
has infinitely many solutions for the variables $x, y, z$, where $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbf{R}$, then the value of $\alpha^2 + 2\beta^2 + \alpha + \beta$ is equal to :
questions.question:
If the matrix equation
x \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} + z \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ \alpha \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ \beta \end{bmatrix}
has infinitely many solutions for the variables $x, y, z$, where $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbf{R}$, then the value of $\alpha^2 + 2\beta^2 + \alpha + \beta$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
The given matrix equation can be written as a system of linear equations:
$x + y + 2z = 1$
$2x + y - z = 4$
$x - y + \alpha z = \beta$

For the system to have infinitely many solutions, we must have $D = D_1 = D_2 = D_3 = 0$.

$D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & \alpha \end{vmatrix} = 1(\alpha - 1) - 1(2\alpha + 1) + 2(-2 - 1) = -\alpha - 8$
Setting $D = 0$, we get $\alpha = -8$.

Now, $D_3 = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & \beta \end{vmatrix} = 1(\beta + 4) - 1(2\beta - 4) + 1(-2 - 1) = -\beta + 5$
Setting $D_3 = 0$, we get $\beta = 5$.

We can verify that for $\alpha = -8$ and $\beta = 5$, $D_1 = 0$ and $D_2 = 0$ as well.

Therefore, the value of the required expression is:
$\alpha^2 + 2\beta^2 + \alpha + \beta = (-8)^2 + 2(5)^2 + (-8) + 5 = 64 + 50 - 3 = 111$.

Answer: 111

questions.question: Let $f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} k+\sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ \sin^2 x & k+\cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ \sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & k+\sin 2x \end{vmatrix}$, where $k$ is a real number. If the maximum value of $f(x)$ over all real $x$ is $96$, then the value of $k$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} k+\sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ \sin^2 x & k+\cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ \sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & k+\sin 2x \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the column operation $C_1 \to C_1 + C_2 + C_3$, the first column becomes:
$C_1 = \begin{bmatrix} k + \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x + \sin 2x \\ \sin^2 x + k + \cos^2 x + \sin 2x \\ \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x + k + \sin 2x \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} k + 1 + \sin 2x \\ k + 1 + \sin 2x \\ k + 1 + \sin 2x \end{bmatrix}$

Taking $(k + 1 + \sin 2x)$ common from $C_1$, we get:
$f(x) = (k + 1 + \sin 2x) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ 1 & k+\cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ 1 & \cos^2 x & k+\sin 2x \end{vmatrix}$

Applying row operations $R_2 \to R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$:
$f(x) = (k + 1 + \sin 2x) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos^2 x & \sin 2x \\ 0 & k & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & k \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along the first column, the determinant is $k^2$.
$\Rightarrow f(x) = k^2(k + 1 + \sin 2x)$

The maximum value of $f(x)$ occurs when $\sin 2x$ is maximum, i.e., $\sin 2x = 1$.
Maximum value $= k^2(k + 1 + 1) = k^2(k + 2)$

Given that the maximum value is $96$:
$k^3 + 2k^2 = 96$
$\Rightarrow k^3 + 2k^2 - 96 = 0$
$\Rightarrow (k - 4)(k^2 + 6k + 24) = 0$

Since $k^2 + 6k + 24 = 0$ has no real roots (discriminant $D = 36 - 96 < 0$), the only real solution is $k = 4$.

Answer: $4$

questions.question:
If the system of linear equations

$x + 4y + (k+4)z = 0$
$x + y + (k+1)z = 0$
$(k-2)x + (3-2k)y = 0$

has a non-trivial solution, then the sum of all possible values of $k$ is
questions.solution:
For a homogeneous system of linear equations to have a non-trivial solution, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 & k+4 \\ 1 & 1 & k+1 \\ k-2 & 3-2k & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying the row operation $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 - R_2$:

$\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & k+1 \\ k-2 & 3-2k & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying the column operation $C_2 \rightarrow C_2 - C_3$:

$\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & -k & k+1 \\ k-2 & 3-2k & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$3 [1(3 - 2k) - (-k)(k - 2)] = 0$

$\Rightarrow 3 - 2k + k^2 - 2k = 0$

$\Rightarrow k^2 - 4k + 3 = 0$

The roots of this quadratic equation are $k = 1$ and $k = 3$.

The sum of all possible values of $k$ is $1 + 3 = 4$.

Answer: $4$

questions.question: If the equation $x \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + y \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} + z \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ a \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 7 \\ b \end{pmatrix}$ has infinitely many solutions for $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}$, then the value of $a+b$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The given matrix equation can be written as a system of linear equations:

$x + 2y + z = 4$
$2x + 3y + z = 7$
$3x + 4y + az = b$

For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & a \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$1(3a - 4) - 2(2a - 3) + 1(8 - 9) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3a - 4 - 4a + 6 - 1 = 0$
$\Rightarrow -a + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow a = 1$

Substituting $a = 1$ into the third equation, the system becomes:
$x + 2y + z = 4$ (i)
$2x + 3y + z = 7$ (ii)
$3x + 4y + z = b$ (iii)

Observe that equation (iii) can be obtained by a linear combination of the first two equations. Specifically, $2 \times \text{(ii)} - \text{(i)}$ gives:
$2(2x + 3y + z) - (x + 2y + z) = 3x + 4y + z$

For the system to be consistent (and thus have infinitely many solutions), the same operation must hold for the constant terms:
$b = 2(7) - 4 = 14 - 4 = 10$

Therefore, $a + b = 1 + 10 = 11$.

Answer: $11$

questions.question:
If the system of linear equations
$x + 2y + 3z = 4$
$2x + 3y + 4z = 5$
$3x + 4y + pz = q$
has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $p + q$ is equal to
questions.solution:
For the system of equations to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & p \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:
$1(3p - 16) - 2(2p - 12) + 3(8 - 9) = 0$
$3p - 16 - 4p + 24 - 3 = 0$
$-p + 5 = 0 \implies p = 5$

For infinitely many solutions, the system must be consistent. This means the third equation must be a linear combination of the first two equations.
Let $R_3 = aR_1 + bR_2$. Comparing the coefficients of $x$ and $y$:
$a + 2b = 3$
$2a + 3b = 4$

Solving these equations, multiply the first by $2$:
$2a + 4b = 6$
Subtracting the second equation gives $b = 2$.
Substituting $b = 2$ into the first equation gives $a = -1$.

Thus, $R_3 = -R_1 + 2R_2$.
Checking the coefficient of $z$: $-1(3) + 2(4) = 5$, which matches $p = 5$.

Applying the same linear combination to the constant terms gives $q$:
$q = -1(4) + 2(5) = -4 + 10 = 6$

Therefore, $p + q = 5 + 6 = 11$.

Answer: $11$

questions.question:
If the system of linear equations
$\begin{aligned} & x + 2y + z = 3 \\ & 3x + y - 2z = 4 \\ & -x + 3y + az = b \end{aligned}$
has infinitely many solutions, and $M$ is a matrix defined as $M = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & b & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $|\text{adj}(M)|$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
For the given system of equations to have infinitely many solutions, we must have $D = D_1 = D_2 = D_3 = 0$.

$D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & a \end{vmatrix} = 1(a + 6) - 2(3a - 2) + 1(9 + 1) = -5a + 20$
Setting $D = 0$, we get $a = 4$.

Now, $D_3 = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 & b \end{vmatrix} = 1(b - 12) - 2(3b + 4) + 3(9 + 1) = -5b + 10$
Setting $D_3 = 0$, we get $b = 2$.

Substitute $a = 4$ and $b = 2$ into the matrix $M$:
$M = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of $M$ is:
$|M| = 4(2 - 1) - 1(1 - 1) + 1(1 - 2) = 4(1) - 0 + 1(-1) = 3$

Using the property of the adjoint of a matrix, for an $n \times n$ matrix $M$, $|\text{adj}(M)| = |M|^{n-1}$.
Here, $n = 3$, so:
$|\text{adj}(M)| = |M|^{3-1} = |M|^2 = 3^2 = 9$.

Answer: 9

questions.question: Let the three planes $P_1 : x + y + z = 1$, $P_2 : x + 2y + \alpha z = 2$, and $P_3 : x + 4y + \alpha^2 z = \beta$ intersect in a line. The sum of all possible values of $(\alpha + \beta)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
For the three planes to intersect in a line, the corresponding system of linear equations must have infinitely many solutions.

This requires the determinant of the coefficient matrix, $D$, to be zero:
$D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 1 & 4 & \alpha^2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Applying $C_2 \rightarrow C_2 - C_1$ and $C_3 \rightarrow C_3 - C_1$:
$D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & \alpha - 1 \\ 1 & 3 & \alpha^2 - 1 \end{vmatrix} = (\alpha^2 - 1) - 3(\alpha - 1) = (\alpha - 1)(\alpha - 2)$

Thus, $D = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 1$ or \alpha = 2$.

For infinitely many solutions, we also need $D_x = D_y = D_z = 0$.

Case 1: $\alpha = 1$
$D_x = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ \beta & 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1(2-4) - 1(2-\beta) + 1(8-2\beta) = 4 - \beta$
Setting $D_x = 0$ gives $\beta = 4$. (One can verify $D_y = D_z = 0$ for $\beta = 4$).
So, one possible pair is $(\alpha, \beta) = (1, 4)$.

Case 2: $\alpha = 2$
$D_y = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & \beta & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 1(8-2\beta) - 1(4-2) + 1(\beta-2) = 4 - \beta$
Setting $D_y = 0$ gives $\beta = 4$. (One can verify $D_x = D_z = 0$ for $\beta = 4$).
So, the other possible pair is $(\alpha, \beta) = (2, 4)$.

The possible values of $(\alpha + \beta)$ are $(1 + 4) = 5$ and $(2 + 4) = 6$.
The sum of all possible values is $5 + 6 = 11$.

Answer: $11$

questions.q: Let $\vec{v}_1 = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{v}_2 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, $\vec{v}_3 = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$, and $\vec{u} = \hat{i} + a\hat{j} + a^2\hat{k}$. If the vector equation $x\vec{v}_1 + y\vec{v}_2 + z\vec{v}_3 = \vec{u}$ has infinitely many solutions for the scalars $x, y, z$, and $\alpha, \beta$ are the possible values of $a$, then the value of $\alpha^4 + \beta^4$ is equal to :
questions.question: Let $\vec{v}_1 = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{v}_2 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, $\vec{v}_3 = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$, and $\vec{u} = \hat{i} + a\hat{j} + a^2\hat{k}$. If the vector equation $x\vec{v}_1 + y\vec{v}_2 + z\vec{v}_3 = \vec{u}$ has infinitely many solutions for the scalars $x, y, z$, and $\alpha, \beta$ are the possible values of $a$, then the value of $\alpha^4 + \beta^4$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
The given vector equation $x\vec{v}_1 + y\vec{v}_2 + z\vec{v}_3 = \vec{u}$ can be written as a system of linear equations by equating the $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ components:
$x + y + z = 1$
$x + 2y + 3z = a$
$x + 5y + 9z = a^2$

For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero, and $\Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0$.
Let us verify the determinant of the coefficient matrix:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 5 & 9 \end{vmatrix} = 1(18 - 15) - 1(9 - 3) + 1(5 - 2) = 3 - 6 + 3 = 0$.

Now, we set $\Delta_z = 0$:
$\Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & a \\ 1 & 5 & a^2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$
$\Rightarrow 1(2a^2 - 5a) - 1(a^2 - a) + 1(5 - 2) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 2a^2 - 5a - a^2 + a + 3 = 0$
$\Rightarrow a^2 - 4a + 3 = 0$
$\Rightarrow (a - 1)(a - 3) = 0$
Thus, the possible values of $a$ are $1$ and $3$.

Let $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 3$.
The value of $\alpha^4 + \beta^4 = 1^4 + 3^4 = 1 + 81 = 82$.

Answer: 82

questions.question:
Consider the system of linear equations:
$x + ay + z = 1$
$ax + y + z = 2$
$x + y + az = b$

The complete set of conditions on $a$ and $b$ for which the system has no solution is
questions.solution:
For the system to have no solution, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero:
$\Delta = egin{vmatrix} 1 & a & 1 \ a & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & a \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant:
$1(a - 1) - a(a^2 - 1) + 1(a - 1) = 0$
$(a - 1)[1 - a(a + 1) + 1] = 0$
$(a - 1)(2 - a - a^2) = 0$
$-(a - 1)^2(a + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow a = 1$ or $a = -2$

Case 1: $a = 1$
The first two equations become $x + y + z = 1$ and $x + y + z = 2$.
These represent parallel, distinct planes and are inherently contradictory. Thus, the system has no solution for any real value of $b$.
Condition: $a = 1$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$.

Case 2: $a = -2$
The system becomes:
$x - 2y + z = 1$
$-2x + y + z = 2$
$x + y - 2z = b$
Adding the first two equations gives $-x - y + 2z = 3$, which can be written as $x + y - 2z = -3$.
For this to contradict the third equation $x + y - 2z = b$, we must have $b eq -3$.
Condition: $a = -2$ and $b eq -3$.

Combining both cases, the complete condition is $a = 1, b \in \mathbb{R}$ or $a = -2, b eq -3$.

Answer: $a = 1, b \in \mathbb{R}$ or $a = -2, b eq -3$

questions.question:
The number of values of $\theta \in (0, 3\pi)$ for which the system of linear equations

$x \cos 3\theta + y \cos 2\theta + z = 0$

$x + y + z = 0$

$2x + 3y + 4z = 0$

has non-trivial solutions is
questions.solution:
For a homogeneous system of linear equations to have non-trivial solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.



$D = \begin{vmatrix} \cos 3\theta & \cos 2\theta & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 0$



Expanding along the first row:



$\cos 3\theta (4 - 3) - \cos 2\theta (4 - 2) + 1 (3 - 2) = 0$



$\Rightarrow \cos 3\theta - 2\cos 2\theta + 1 = 0$



Using multiple angle identities $\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$ and $\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$:



$\Rightarrow (4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta) - 2(2\cos^2\theta - 1) + 1 = 0$



$\Rightarrow 4\cos^3\theta - 4\cos^2\theta - 3\cos\theta + 3 = 0$



$\Rightarrow 4\cos^2\theta(\cos\theta - 1) - 3(\cos\theta - 1) = 0$



$\Rightarrow (\cos\theta - 1)(4\cos^2\theta - 3) = 0$



This gives $\cos\theta = 1$ or $\cos\theta = \pm \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.



We need to find the number of solutions in the interval $(0, 3\pi)$.



For $\cos\theta = 1$: $\theta = 2\pi$ (1 solution)



For $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$: $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}, \dfrac{13\pi}{6}$ (3 solutions)



For $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$: $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{17\pi}{6}$ (3 solutions)



Total number of solutions = $1 + 3 + 3 = 7$.



Answer: $7$

questions.question:
The system of linear equations
$x + y + z = 1$
$2x + 3y + \sin(\theta)z = 2$
$3x + 4y + (\cos(2\theta) + 2\sin(\theta) + 1)z = 4$
has no solution. If $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$ and the sum of all possible values of $\theta$ is $\dfrac{k\pi}{2}$, then the value of $k$ is
questions.solution:
For the system to have no solution, $\Delta = 0$ and at least one of $\Delta_x, \Delta_y, \Delta_z \neq 0$.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & \sin(\theta) \\ 3 & 4 & \cos(2\theta) + 2\sin(\theta) + 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Applying $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - 3R_1$:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \sin(\theta) - 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \cos(2\theta) + 2\sin(\theta) - 2 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along the first column:
$\Delta = 1 \cdot (\cos(2\theta) + 2\sin(\theta) - 2 - (\sin(\theta) - 2))$
$\Delta = \cos(2\theta) + \sin(\theta)$

Setting $\Delta = 0$:
$\cos(2\theta) + \sin(\theta) = 0$
$1 - 2\sin^2(\theta) + \sin(\theta) = 0$
$2\sin^2(\theta) - \sin(\theta) - 1 = 0$
$(2\sin(\theta) + 1)(\sin(\theta) - 1) = 0$

$\sin(\theta) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin(\theta) = 1$

For $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$:
If $\sin(\theta) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$
If $\sin(\theta) = 1$, $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Sum of all values of $\theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} + \dfrac{11\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 3\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{7\pi}{2}$

Also, for these values, $\Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 1 \neq 0$, confirming the system has no solution.

Comparing with $\dfrac{k\pi}{2}$, we get $k = 7$.

Answer: $7$

questions.question: Let $f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} a^2 + \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{x^2} & ab & ac \\ ab & b^2 + \dfrac{e^x-1}{x} & bc \\ ac & bc & c^2 + \dfrac{\tan x}{x} \end{vmatrix}$, where $x \neq 0$. If $a = 2$, $b = 3$, and $c = 4$, then the value of $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
We know the standard limits: $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{x^2} = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^x-1}{x} = 1$, and $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\tan x}{x} = 1$.

Applying the limit $x \to 0$ to the entries of the determinant, we get:
$\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} a^2+1 & ab & ac \\ ab & b^2+1 & bc \\ ac & bc & c^2+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Multiply $R_1, R_2, R_3$ by $a, b, c$ respectively and divide the determinant by $abc$:
$\dfrac{1}{abc} \begin{vmatrix} a(a^2+1) & a^2b & a^2c \\ ab^2 & b(b^2+1) & b^2c \\ ac^2 & bc^2 & c(c^2+1) \end{vmatrix}$

Taking $a, b, c$ common from $C_1, C_2, C_3$ respectively:
$\begin{vmatrix} a^2+1 & a^2 & a^2 \\ b^2 & b^2+1 & b^2 \\ c^2 & c^2 & c^2+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the row operation $R_1 \to R_1 + R_2 + R_3$:
$\begin{vmatrix} a^2+b^2+c^2+1 & a^2+b^2+c^2+1 & a^2+b^2+c^2+1 \\ b^2 & b^2+1 & b^2 \\ c^2 & c^2 & c^2+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Taking $(a^2+b^2+c^2+1)$ common from $R_1$:
$(a^2+b^2+c^2+1) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ b^2 & b^2+1 & b^2 \\ c^2 & c^2 & c^2+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Applying $C_2 \to C_2 - C_1$ and $C_3 \to C_3 - C_1$:
$(a^2+b^2+c^2+1) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ b^2 & 1 & 0 \\ c^2 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = a^2+b^2+c^2+1$

Substitute $a=2, b=3, c=4$:
$\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 + 1 = 4 + 9 + 16 + 1 = 30$.

Answer: 30

Expanding along the first row:

Then $c_2 = 4 - 2(1) = 2$.
Checking the coefficient of $z$: $1(3) + 2(-1) = 1$, which matches $\alpha = 1$.

Applying this linear combination to the constant terms to find $\beta$:
$1(5) + 2(\beta) = 11$
$2\beta = 6 \implies \beta = 3$

Now, substitute $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 3$ into matrix $M$:

Calculate the determinant of $M$:

questions.solution:
For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero, and the augmented matrices must also have zero determinants. This implies that one equation is a linear combination of the other two.

Observing the coefficients of $x$, $y$, and $z$, we can see that the third row is the sum of the first two rows:
$(x + y + z) + (2x + y - z) = 3x + 2y$

For the system to be consistent and have infinitely many solutions, the same linear combination must apply to the constant terms. Therefore:
$k = 4 + 3 = 7$

We are given that $(x_0, y_0, 2)$ is a solution. Substituting $z = 2$ into the first two equations:
$x_0 + y_0 + 2 = 4 \Rightarrow x_0 + y_0 = 2$
$2x_0 + y_0 - 2 = 3 \Rightarrow 2x_0 + y_0 = 5$

Subtracting the first equation from the second yields:
$x_0 = 3$

Substituting $x_0 = 3$ back into $x_0 + y_0 = 2$ gives:
$3 + y_0 = 2 \Rightarrow y_0 = -1$

Finally, the required sum is:
$k + x_0 + y_0 = 7 + 3 + (-1) = 9$

Answer: $9$

For the system to have no solution, we must have $\Delta = 0$ and at least one of $\Delta_x, \Delta_y, \Delta_z \neq 0$.



$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 & 13 + \cos 2\theta \end{vmatrix}$



Expanding along the first row:



$\Delta = 1(39 + 3\cos 2\theta - 35) - 1(26 + 2\cos 2\theta - 20) + 1(14 - 12)$



$\Rightarrow \Delta = (4 + 3\cos 2\theta) - (6 + 2\cos 2\theta) + 2 = \cos 2\theta$



Setting $\Delta = 0$ gives $\cos 2\theta = 0$. For $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, $2\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$, which gives $2\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.



Thus, $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.



Now we evaluate $\Delta_z$:



$\Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 7 & 3 + \sqrt{2}\cos\theta \end{vmatrix}$



$\Delta_z = 1(9 + 3\sqrt{2}\cos\theta - 14) - 1(6 + 2\sqrt{2}\cos\theta - 8) + 1(14 - 12)$



$\Rightarrow \Delta_z = (-5 + 3\sqrt{2}\cos\theta) - (-2 + 2\sqrt{2}\cos\theta) + 2 = \sqrt{2}\cos\theta - 1$



For $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \Delta_z = 1 - 1 = 0$. (This leads to infinitely many solutions).



For $\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \Delta_z = -1 - 1 = -2 \neq 0$. (This leads to no solution).



Hence, the only value of $\theta$ for which the system has no solution is $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.



The sum of all such values is $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.



Answer: $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

Answer: $784$
